Family open work permits are limited to spouses of temporary foreign workers who are employed in

* TEER 0 or 1 occupations, or

o * These include occupations in the natural and applied sciences, construction, health care, natural resources, education, sports and military sectors. The full list will be available on January 21, 2025.

In addition, the principal temporary foreign worker must also have at least 16 months remaining on their work permit at the time when their spouse applies for the open work permit. Thank you very much for your response, particularly to Question 1 - that was very helpful and Iappreciate it. For Question 2, would your analysis that the "Temporary public policy to exempt foreign nationals in Canada from

## certain requirements when changing employment" (the “Policy”) doesn't apply to a BOWP application change

Immigration, Réfugiés and Citizenship Canada et Citoyenneté Canada Information disclosed under the Access to Information Act

- * The BOWP applicant did in-fact intend to work for a new employer, secured a job with that employer, and included a job offer letter with their BOWP application.
My position is that a BOWP does fall within the Policy for the following reasons:

Email Statement 1: "The public policy is for applicants that meet the conditions, including (but limited to) submitting a work permit application or work permit renewal application under subsection 201(1) of the

# Regulations to perform work described in as per paragraphs 200(1)(c)(ii.1) or 200(1)(c)(ii) of the

Regulations, and that intends to work for a new employer and/or occupation as specified by the job offer included in their work permit application, so that they may work for a new employer while waiting on a

# decision on their application."

- A BOWP application falls under R200(1)(c)(ii.1) as the applicant intends to perform work described in R205 and has an offer of employment to perform work and that offer is genuine. Specifically, a BOWP application falls under R205(a) and is part of the International Mobility Program. It is a work permit that would create or maintain significant benefits or opportunities for Canadian citizens or permanent residents since it is a work permit to allow skilled workers to work in Canada and contribute to Canada's economy while their PR application is in process. The R205(a) exemption code is A75 as confirmed in this IRCC Page: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-) manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/foreign-workers/exemption- codes.html#r205
Email Statement 2: "Noting that an applicant applying for a fully open work permit would not be covered by the public policy as they cannot fulfill the condition to intend to work for a new employer and/or occupation as specified by the job offer included in their work permit application. Only workers applying for an employer specific work permit can fulfill the requirement of having secured a job offer under the terms of either the Temporary Foreign Worker Program or International Mobility Program."

- Iwould respond that just because a BOWP application doesn't REQUIRE a job offer to be approved doesn't mean an applicant can't intend to work for a specific employer and obtain a job offer from that employer and include that job offer with their BOWP application.
- The wording of the Policy's eligibility criteria is that the applicant INTENDS to work for a new employer, not that they must work for a new/specific employer.
The Policy's eligibility requirements are as follows and I would argue that a BOWP can fall within this eligibility requirements under certain circumstances (for example where a BOWP is being applied for in a situation where the applicant is in Canada on an LMlA-based work permit and needs to move to a new employer not listed on the LMIA-based work permit). In that situation purpose and intention of the Policy would clearly apply to allow the applicant to begin working for that employer while their BOWP application is in process.

Good day, Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox. Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries but have provided the following information as guidance. If you have case specific questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit the IRCC Web form. Please see our response to your question. *** Q1: For the purposes of “Work Location” definition, does that mean that the “Work Location” does not change as long as the new employer is also located within the same city-in this case Victoria BC? In other words, is the correct understanding that “Work Location” does not need to be the exact same address as the original employer as long as it is within the same city as stated on the work permit?

Response 1:

Please be advised that IRCC cannot provide case-specific advice. Therefore, our response reflects general information on work permits. While we cannot provide case-specific recommendations or immigration advice on work permit options for the scenario you describe, please refer to the Temporary Workers General Eligibility Requirements in order to determine the work permit options available under the Temporary Foreign Worker Program and the International Mobility Program. All information was correct at the time/date the response was sent.

With regards to work location, it depends on the conditions of the work permit.

If the employment location is specified under either “Conditions” or “Remarks/observations” or if it states “Not authorized to work in any location other than stated” then the work permit holder must only work at the location specified on the permit.

With regards to this general enquiry, we also invite you also to review the page regarding Employer name changes and corporate restructurings-Canada.ca for detailed information on when a new work permit Is required in the context of Corporate restructurings and company mergers.

Q2: If the TFW needs a new work permit, and they have already applied for PR after receiving an ITA for CEC, can they alternatively apply for a Bridging Open Work Permit (BOWP) and use the "Temporary public policy to exempt foreign nationals in Canada from certain requirements when changing employment” (the “Policy") to apply for a BOWP and begin to work for the new employer before a decision is made on their BOWP?

Link to Policy: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/mandate/policies-operational-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/mandate/policies-operational-) instructions-agreements/public-policies/changing-employment.html

Response 2:

The public policy is for applicants that meet the conditions, including (but limited to) submitting a work permit application or work permit renewal application under subsection 201(1) of the Regúlations to perform work described in as per paragraphs 200(1)(c)(ii.1) or 200(1)(c)(iii) of the Regulations, and that intends to work for a new employer and/or occupation as specified by the job offer included in their work permit application, so that they may work for a new employer while waiting on a decision on their application.

000020

Immigration, Refugees Immigration, Réfugiés and Citizenship Canadaet Citoyenneté Canada

s.19(1)Information disclosed under the Access to Information Act
L'information divulguée en vertu de la oi sur l’accès à Finformation

The objectives of this public policy are to allow temporary foreign workers already in Canada who are changing jobs or employers, and who have secured a job offer under the terms of either the Temporary Foreign Worker Program or International Mobility Program, to more quickly begin work in advance of a final decision on the work permit application.

Noting that an applicant applying for a fully open work permit would not be covered by the public policy as they cannot fulfill the condition to intend to work for a new employer and/or occupation as specified by the job offer included in their work permit application. Only workers applying for an employer specific work permit can fulfill the requirement of having secured a job offer under the terms of either the Temporary Foreign Worker Program or International Mobility Program.

Q3: If the TFW applies for a BOWP and rely on the Policy, would they need to wait for any communication from IRCC before they are authorized to work in Canada under this Policy before a decision has been made?

Response 3:

See above response. Open work permit applicants are not covered by the public policy.

We hope this information is of assistance.

# Please see our response to your question.

Adults living in separate locations are required to submit applications individually. Each application should include all required documents, have its own receipt and should be mailed individually per the instructions available online. Submitting applications for multiple adults who, although related, do not live in the same household could cause unexpected delays.

Proof of citizenship applications should only be sent together if the family members are part of the same household. For example, this is commonly done when a parent applies for proof of citizenship for multiple minor children at the same time.

In the scenario explained below, to assuage any concerns, a letter can be sent with the son's application explaining that his father's application is being submitted from Mexico. ***

1) Under current CUAET public policy-can a person apply for a new study permit (never held a study permit before) if the person initially entered Canada on a CUAÉT work permit before March 31, 2024, currently holds a CUAET work Response: Yes, Ukrainians and their family members who were approved under CUAET and who arrived in Canada on or before March 31, 2024, may apply from within Canada by March 31, 2026, for a new study permit, a new open work permit or for a renewal of their current work permit, subject to standard fees. While the public policy does not allow clients to apply for a study permit renewal, Ukrainians who are in Canada and already hold a valid work permit, including those under the CUAET public policy, may choose to apply for a study permit extension through the regular application For regularly updated information on immigration measures for Ukrainians and their families, please visit: Immigration
2) If the answer to the above question is "yes" - is the person under the CUAET policy exempt from the requirement of Response: Yes, Ukrainians and their family members who were approved under CUAET applying for initial study permits are exempted from the requirements to provide a provincial attestation letter (PAL) or territorial attestation letter
3) If the answer to the first question is "yes" - is Acceptance Letter from a DLl generally required to apply for a study Response: Yes, aside from the requirements exempted in this public policy, applicants must meet all other standard eligibility and admissibility requirements for the issuance of a study permit. Good day, Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox. Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries but have provided the following information as guidance. If you have case specific questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit the IRCC Web form. Please see our response to your question. *** The current Economic Mobility Pathways Pilot (EMPP) Public Policies requires a principal applicant to submit one of the following documents with their application for permanent residence:

- * a positive Refugee Status Determination (RSD) from either the UNHCR, or a refugee-hosting state;
- * proof of being registered or recorded as a person of concern by the UNHCR, if a positive RSD has not been obtained yet or is not available in the state where the foreign national is residing at the time of their application;
- * a refugee certificate with the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA);
- * proof of being registered or recorded as a person of concern by the UNRWA, if a refugee certificate has not been obtained yet;
* a valid Trusted Partner Referral Letter issued by an organization with a Trusted Partner Arrangement with IRCC; OR
- * proof of having Temporary Protected Status issued by the hosting state where the foreign national is residing at the time their application for permanent residence is received; and to be a person in respect of whom there is no reasonable prospect, within a reasonable period, of a durable solution in a country other than Canada, namely: (i) voluntary repatriation or resettlement in their country of nationality or habitual residence, or (ii) resettlement or an offer of resettlement in another country, as set out in paragraph 139 (1)(d) of the Regulations.
Under the current EMPP, IRCC officers only assess principal applicants for durable solutions when they submit a Temporary Protected Status document to IRCC in order to meet the eligibility criteria. A principal applicant who has provided one of the other documents such as a refugee certificate with the ÜNRWA is not assessed by IRCC for a durable solution regardless of where they live or their citizenship(s). Applicants will still have to meet all other eligibility and admissibility requirements under the EMPP to be approved for permanent residence.

It is also important to keep in mind that the EMPP public policy intent is to help skilled refugees and other displaced persons immigrate to Canada. In order to maintain this intent, persons who already have a durable solution and are no ionger displaced or in need of protection should be encouraged to consider other economic programs to immigrate to Canada.

Please note that we do not respond to case specific questions. Each case is assessed by an officer considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to them. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements of the program they are applying under.

We trust this information will be of assistance to you.

# Bonjour,

Je suis CRÉÉ no, je travaille à. J’aimerais avoir des précisions concernant la nécessité, ou pas, de faire les examens médicaux aux fins de l’immigration afin d’effectuer des stages pour nos étudiants de l’École de travail social et de criminologie.

Les stages ont principalement lieu dans trois secteurs :

1. 1. Centres intégrés de santé et de services sociaux (CiSSS) et centres intégrés universitaires de santé et de services sociaux (CIUSSS): essentiellement en Direction de la protection de la jeunesse (DPJ), clientèle: enfants, adolescents et adultes.
2. 2. Milieux judiciaires : maisons de transition, prisons/pénitenciers, bureaux de libération conditionnelle, bureau de probation, agents de programme.
3. 3. Milieux communautaires : très diversifiés, tous types de clientèles. Problématiques : toxicomanie, itinérance,

## Sent: Tuesday, November 25, 2025 2:06:18 PM

To: Cc: Immigration Representatives / Représentants immigration (IRCC) Subject: FW: For review: FW: Policy clarification request – EMPP permanent residents and travel to country of nationality-REP-B-2025-2125 - Due 1-Dec-25 Importance: Normal Sensitivity: None

Good day,

## Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.

Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-

## specific inquiries but have provided the following information as guidance. If you have case specific

questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit the IRCC Web form. Please see our response to your question. *** The EMPP Public Policies do not restrict travel for EMPP Permanent Residents (PRs) after their arrival in Canada including to their country of origin. As such there may be no impact to their Permanent Resident status in Canada due to travelling to their country of origin after they arrive in Canada. However, it should be noted that travelling to their country of origin is not something that the department encourages due to the potential safety and/or security concerns for the client. Furthermore, it is important to be aware that as with any case, should information come to light that a client may

## have misrepresented or withheld material facts in their permanent resident application, an investigation may be

launched which could result in enforcement action being taken including the loss of their permanent resident status.

Additionally, if clients are looking to travel internationally after their arrival in Canada, they will need to ensure that they have the required travel documents to do so. For example, if a client used a Single Journey Travel Documents issued by the department, to travel to Canada, they will not be able to use that document to travel from Canada after their arrival.

Clients may need to apply for Certificates of Identity after they arrive to enable international travel. It is important to note that some countries may not accept the Certificate of Identity as a valid travel document and clients should check with the consulate or embassy of the country that they wish to visit before travelling.

***

Thank you kindly,
